lead: A limit answers a narrow question: as x gets close to a number a, what value does f(x) get close to? The function may never reach that value, or may not even be defined at a. Continuity turns this into a stronger promise: the graph has no break, jump or hole at a. Limits are the base of the derivative, of numerical tolerances in code, and of every smooth curve in physics and engineering.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1: reading a graph, domain and range, and piecewise definitions.

blocks.text: Write lim<sub>x→a</sub> f(x) = L. Read it: the limit of f(x) as x tends to a equals L. L is the single real number that f(x) approaches when x is close to a but not equal to a. The point a itself is excluded.
The left limit lim<sub>x→a⁻</sub> f(x) uses x < a. The right limit lim<sub>x→a⁺</sub> f(x) uses x > a. A two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and are equal.
lim<sub>x→a</sub> f(x) = L ⇔ lim<sub>x→a⁻</sub> f(x) = L and lim<sub>x→a⁺</sub> f(x) = L
blocks.where: L is the common one-sided value; ⇔ means if and only if; a is the point being approached.

blocks.text: Limit notation ignores the value at a. A function can have a limit at a point where it is undefined. The figure shows a jump: the left branch ends at y = 1, while the right branch starts at y = 3.

sections.h3: Limit laws and limits at infinity

blocks.text: Limit laws split a complicated limit into simple ones. They hold when every limit on the right side exists as a real number.

items: Sum: lim(f + g) = lim f + lim g.
Constant multiple: lim(cf) = c lim f.
Quotient: lim(f/g) = (lim f)/(lim g), if lim g ≠ 0.
Power: lim(f<sup>n</sup>) = (lim f)<sup>n</sup>, and similarly for roots where defined.

blocks.text: For a polynomial p(x), direct substitution works: limx→a p(x) = p(a). For a rational function, substitute if the denominator is not zero. If you get 0/0, factor or simplify first; see Chapter 1.6.

At infinity, lim<sub>x→∞</sub> 1/x = 0 and lim<sub>x→−∞</sub> 1/x = 0. For a rational function, divide numerator and denominator by the highest power of x in the denominator. The limit is the ratio of leading coefficients if the degrees match, 0 if the denominator degree is larger, and unbounded if the numerator degree is larger. If lim<sub>x→∞</sub> f(x) = L, the line y = L is a horizontal asymptote.
An infinite limit such as lim<sub>x→0⁺</sub> 1/x = ∞ means 1/x grows without bound. The symbol ∞ is not a real limit value. The line x = 0 is a vertical asymptote.

For a bounded function near a, the limit superior is the largest value approached and the limit inferior the smallest. A limit exists exactly when these two are equal. Sequences use the same idea; see Unit 3, Sequences and Infinite Series.

sections.h3: Continuity at a point and on an interval

blocks.text: A function f is continuous at x = a when three conditions hold.

items: lim<sub>x→a</sub> f(x) exists, so the two one-sided limits agree.

blocks.text: If any condition fails, f is discontinuous at a. Continuity on an open interval (p, q) means continuity at every point inside. On a closed interval [p, q], also require the one-sided limits at the endpoints to match the endpoint values: lim<sub>x→p⁺</sub> f(x) = f(p) and lim<sub>x→q⁻</sub> f(x) = f(q).
Polynomials are continuous everywhere. Rational functions are continuous wherever the denominator is not zero. sin x and cos x are continuous everywhere, and e<sup>x</sup> is continuous everywhere.

items: Removable discontinuity: the limit exists, but f(a) is missing or different. The graph has a hole.
Jump discontinuity: the one-sided limits exist but differ. The graph breaks vertically.
Infinite discontinuity: f(x) grows without bound near a. The graph has a vertical asymptote.

blocks.text: Continuity is necessary for differentiability but not sufficient: |x| is continuous at 0 and not differentiable there. See Chapter 1.3.

figure.caption: At x = 1 the left branch reaches y = 1 and the right branch starts at y = 3, so the one-sided limits differ and the graph jumps.

spec.aria: The graph has a break at x equals 1: the left branch rises to y equals 1, and the right branch is the flat line y equals 3.

examples.question: Let f(x) = x² for x < 1 and f(x) = 3 for x ≥ 1. Find lim<sub>x→1⁻</sub> f(x), lim<sub>x→1⁺</sub> f(x), and f(1). Does lim<sub>x→1</sub> f(x) exist? Is f continuous at x = 1?
steps: For x < 1 use f(x) = x². As x→1 from the left, x²→1² = 1. The left limit is 1.
For x > 1 use f(x) = 3. The constant 3 does not change, so the right limit is 3.
The one-sided limits are 1 and 3. They are not equal, so the two-sided limit lim<sub>x→1</sub> f(x) does not exist.
At x = 1 the rule x ≥ 1 applies, so f(1) = 3.
Continuity at x = 1 needs the two-sided limit to exist and equal f(1). The limit does not exist, so f is not continuous at x = 1. This is a jump discontinuity.
examples.answer: Left limit = 1, right limit = 3, f(1) = 3, the two-sided limit does not exist, and f is not continuous at x = 1 (jump discontinuity).
examples.check:
left = 1 ** 2
right = 3
f_at_1 = 3
print(left)
print(right)
print(f_at_1)

traps: A limit can exist where f(a) is undefined. Do not plug in a first and declare the limit missing; look at nearby values.
Do not write lim f(x) = ∞ and then treat ∞ as a number. It only says f(x) grows without bound; the limit as a real number does not exist.
For a piecewise function, the branch with ≥ or ≤ gives f(a), but each one-sided limit uses x < a or x > a, not the value at a.
Cancelling (x − a) in a ratio changes the domain at x = a. The simplified expression is valid only for x ≠ a; the limit can still exist.

quiz.q: State the three conditions for f to be continuous at x = a.
quiz.a: f(a) is defined; lim<sub>x→a</sub> f(x) exists; the limit equals f(a).

quiz.q: Explain why a function can have a limit at a point where it is not defined.
quiz.a: The limit uses values of f near a, not f(a). A hole at a does not change the nearby values.

quiz.q: At x = 1 the left limit is 2 and the right limit is 5. What is the two-sided limit?
quiz.a: It does not exist, because the one-sided limits are not equal.

quiz.q: f(x) = x + 1 for x < 2, and f(x) = 5 for x ≥ 2. Find the left and right limits at x = 2, and decide continuity at x = 2.
quiz.a: Left limit = 2 + 1 = 3. Right limit = 5. f(2) = 5. The two-sided limit does not exist, so f is not continuous at x = 2 (jump).

quiz.q: Find a so that f(x) = x² for x < 2 and f(x) = ax for x ≥ 2 is continuous at x = 2.
quiz.a: Left limit = 2² = 4. Right limit = 2a. f(2) = 2a. Set 2a = 4, so a = 2.

quiz.q: A graph has a hole at (3, 4), and f(3) = 1. Is f continuous at x = 3? Which condition fails?
quiz.a: No. The limit is 4, f(3) = 1, and 4 ≠ 1. The equality condition fails; this is a removable discontinuity.

quiz.q: Give an example of a function that has a limit at x = 0 but is not continuous there.
quiz.a: f(x) = x for x ≠ 0, and f(0) = 1. The limit is 0, but f(0) = 1, so f is not continuous at 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. The formal ε–δ definition turns “gets close” into inequalities: for every ε > 0 there is δ > 0 such that 0 < |x − a| < δ implies |f(x) − L| < ε. Numerical libraries use the same idea with floating-point tolerances. Control systems check continuity before applying linear approximations; signal processing uses one-sided limits at switching instants. Search: epsilon-delta definition, one-sided limits, removable discontinuity.
